title: Bach: Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, Third Movement — Guided Listening
content_html:
Bach: Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, Third Movement

A concerto grosso from about 1721: three soloists — flute, violin and obbligato harpsichord, the concertino — set against a string ripieno with continuo. D major, Allegro, 2/4, and built as a fugue with the swing of a gigue.

Bach sent the six concertos to the Margrave of Brandenburg unasked, hoping for work. The harpsichord is what makes this one famous: usually the accompanist, here a soloist.

Press play and the cards follow the music. Tap a number to jump.

1 · Three voices, one subject

The movement opens with the concertino alone. The violin states the subject; the flute answers with the same tune at bar 3; the harpsichord takes it at bar 9. Each entry overlaps the last — this is a fugal exposition, and the texture is contrapuntal from the first bar.

Listen for: count the three entries. Hear how the harpsichord arrives as a melody, not as chords underneath.

2 · The ripieno joins

At bar 29 the full strings enter and the sound suddenly thickens. This is the first full ritornello: the theme in the whole ensemble, in the home key of D major. From here the movement alternates tutti ritornellos with lighter episodes for the soloists.

Listen for: the jump in volume and weight when the strings arrive. That contrast between concertino and ripieno is the sound of a concerto grosso.

3 · Into the minor

Bar 79 begins the middle section in B minor, the relative minor. The mood lightens and darkens at once: the concertino dominates, short ideas are repeated in sequence, and the music modulates through related keys before working its way home.

Listen for: the shift from bright major to minor, and the same short motif climbing or falling step by step.

4 · The harpsichord leads

Deep in the B section the harpsichord takes over with running semiquaver figuration while flute and violin drop back. In 1721 a harpsichord was a continuo instrument that filled in harmony; giving it virtuosic solo writing like this was new, and it is why this concerto is called the first keyboard concerto.

Listen for: the plucked, bright tone cutting through, and the trills and ornaments decorating the line.

5 · Da capo

At bar 233 the opening comes back exactly: violin, flute, harpsichord, then the ripieno at bar 261. That makes the whole movement ternary — A (bars 1–78), B (79–232), A again (233–310) — with a fugal ritornello inside each A. Two structures at once: a fugue and ritornello form, framed as da capo.

Listen for: the moment it feels like the piece has started again. It has.

6 · The finish

The last ritornello drives through sequences to a perfect cadence in D major. Throughout, the harmony is functional — chords built on the tonic and dominant, moving with purpose — and the running quavers and semiquavers never let up. That unbroken motion, in a light 2/4, is what gives the movement its gigue-like lilt.

Listen for: the pull towards the final chord, and how firmly it lands.

Say it precisely in the exam

Genre: concerto grosso. Forces: concertino of flute, violin and obbligato harpsichord; ripieno strings with continuo. Key: D major, moving to B minor in the middle section. Metre and tempo: 2/4, Allegro, gigue-like. Structure: ternary, A B A with a da capo, each A built as a fugal ritornello. Texture: contrapuntal and imitative, tutti against soloists. Harmony: functional, perfect cadences, sequences. Context: 1721, dedicated unasked to the Margrave of Brandenburg; the harpsichord as a soloist was new.

Answers score when they tie a term to a moment you can hear. “Ritornello” alone earns little; “the ripieno enters at bar 29 with the subject, in the tonic” earns the mark.
exam_tip_html: When asked to describe the structure of this movement, do not stop at ‘ritornello form’. Name the fugal exposition (violin, then flute at bar 3, then harpsichord at bar 9), the ripieno entry at bar 29, the B minor middle section from bar 79, and the exact da capo at bar 233. Bar numbers and instruments turn a label into a mark.
conclusion_html: You can now hear the six landmarks of the finale — the fugal entries, the ripieno’s arrival, the turn to B minor, the harpsichord’s solo episode, the da capo and the final cadence — and name the genre, forces, key, metre, structure and texture behind each one. The next lesson goes deeper into the texture, tonality and melodic writing across the whole movement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Bach's dedication of the Brandenburg Concertos to the Margrave of Brandenburg is described as 'unsolicited'.
practice_questions.marks: One mark: not commissioned. One mark: sent in hope of patronage, payment or a post.

practice_questions.text: Identify the three instruments that make up the concertino group in Brandenburg Concerto No. 5.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for flute, violin and harpsichord.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the harpsichord's role in this concerto differs from its usual Baroque function.
practice_questions.marks: Usual role: continuo, realising harmony from the bass line. Here: a soloist in the concertino with virtuosic figuration. Credit reference to it being seen as the first keyboard concerto.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the third movement opens, referring to the order of instrumental entries and the texture.
practice_questions.marks: Fugal exposition; concertino alone; violin first, flute at bar 3, harpsichord at bar 9; imitative or contrapuntal texture; ripieno enters at bar 29.

practice_questions.text: Define ritornello form and explain how it is combined with ternary form in this movement.
practice_questions.marks: Ritornello: recurring tutti passage alternating with solo episodes, returning in related keys. Ternary: A (1-78), B (79-232, B minor), A repeated from bar 233 (da capo). Each A section is a fugal ritornello.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by describing the finale's rhythmic character as 'gigue-like'?
practice_questions.marks: A lively, dance-like lilt; continuous running quavers and semiquavers; light 2/4 Allegro with the character of a Baroque gigue.

glossary_terms.definition: A Baroque genre contrasting a small group of soloists with a larger ensemble
The small group of solo instruments in a concerto grosso
The larger body of strings and continuo in a concerto grosso, also called the tutti
A Baroque accompanying part, usually harpsichord and bass instrument, realising harmony from a bass line
A Baroque structure where a recurring theme alternates with contrasting episodes for soloists
Describing music built from imitative entries of a theme between different voices or instruments
A virtuosic solo passage, often unaccompanied, showcasing a performer's technical skill
A lively Baroque dance in compound or triple-based rhythm, often used to close a suite or movement
A formal inscription offering a musical work to a patron, often in hope of favour or employment
A compositional technique where a melodic idea is repeated in different parts shortly after its first statement

description: Listen through the finale of Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 5 with six numbered landmarks: the fugal entries, the ripieno's arrival, the B minor middle section, the harpsichord's solo episode, the da capo and the close.

flashcard_questions.a: Nobody commissioned them. Bach sent the set to the Margrave of Brandenburg in 1721 hoping for patronage or a post, and there is no evidence they were played at his court.
flashcard_questions.q: Why is Bach's dedication of the Brandenburg Concertos described as 'unsolicited'?

flashcard_questions.a: The concertino (soloists): flute, violin and obbligato harpsichord. The ripieno (tutti): the string ensemble with continuo.
flashcard_questions.q: What are the two groups in a concerto grosso, and who is in each here?
Which three instruments form the concertino in Brandenburg Concerto No. 5?

flashcard_questions.a: It is treated as a virtuosic soloist rather than a continuo accompanist, which is why the work is often called the first keyboard concerto.
flashcard_questions.q: What is unusual about the harpsichord's role in this concerto?

flashcard_questions.a: With a fugal exposition for the concertino alone: the violin states the subject, the flute answers at bar 3 and the harpsichord enters at bar 9; the ripieno joins at bar 29.
flashcard_questions.q: How does the third movement open?

flashcard_questions.a: Ternary (A B A) with a da capo: A bars 1 to 78, B bars 79 to 232 in B minor, A repeated exactly from bar 233. Each A section is a fugal ritornello.
flashcard_questions.q: Describe the overall structure of the third movement.
